body.objective: Students will be able to use criteria to evaluate work.
body.iCan: I can use criteria to evaluate work.
successCriteria: I can use criteria and a rubric to evaluate a product
I can give and use specific feedback
body.hook: Before a product reaches a store shelf, someone checks it against a list of requirements. In a CTS lab, that someone is you. Evaluating your own work honestly is what makes the next project better.

study.title: Is It Good Enough?
study.question: How do I judge my work fairly and make it better?
study.passage:
Part 1, Criteria (10 minutes): As a class, list criteria for your project type. Example for a wooden box: accurate dimensions (±1 mm), square corners, tight joints, smooth finish with no tear-out, safe (no splinters or sharp edges). Example for muffins: even size, golden colour, domed tops, moist crumb, cooked through, clean presentation.
Part 2, Rubric (10 minutes): Build a four-level rubric for each criterion: 4 Exceeds, 3 Meets, 2 Approaching, 1 Beginning. Describe what each level looks like.
Part 3, Self-evaluate (10 minutes): Score your own project with evidence ("Corners measured 89° and 90°, so Meets").
Part 4, Peer feedback (15 minutes): In pairs, use "Glow and Grow": one specific strength and one specific suggestion, linked to criteria.
Part 5, Improvement plan (10 minutes): Choose the two lowest criteria and write one action for each ("Use a try square before gluing to check 90°").
study.source: Original evaluation task written for this lesson.
steps: Give and receive Glow and Grow feedback
discussion: Was your self-score higher or lower than your peer's? Why?
Why is evidence important in evaluation?
Which improvement will have the biggest impact?
study.product: Submit a completed rubric with self- and peer scores, evidence for each criterion, and a two-step improvement plan.

examples.title: Criterion
examples.problem: Turn "looks good" into a criterion for a T-shirt print.
examples.answer: Print is centred within 5 mm and has no smudges or gaps

examples.title: Evidence
examples.problem: Support a score of 2 for "even muffin size."
examples.answer: Muffins ranged from 55 g to 80 g, so sizes were uneven

examples.title: Glow and Grow
examples.answer: Glow: title is clear from 3 m away. Grow: the date is hard to find; make it larger

examples.title: Improvement
examples.problem: The finish was rough. Write an action.
examples.answer: Sand with 120 then 220 grit along the grain before finishing
examples.explore: How will you know it worked?

practice.q: Name two criteria for a sewn bag.
practice.a: Even seams, secure stitching, correct size, neat finish.

practice.q: Why might self-scores differ from peer scores?
practice.a: People see their own work differently; evidence helps resolve it.

practice.q: Why focus improvement on the two lowest criteria?
practice.a: They have the biggest effect on overall quality.

practice.q: How do industries use criteria like a rubric?
practice.a: Quality control checks products against specifications.
For example: the joints have gaps over 1 mm; clamp longer while gluing.
